stories.title: Anthropic releases FlashProve, an open-source (Apache 2.0) research prototype for 'provable inference': zkSNARK proofs that a response came from a committed model without revealing its weights; Claude helped build it; on one H100 it proves a 400B Llama 4 Maverick MoE at ~110 tokens/s (~19MB per 1,024 tokens, ~70-95x the GPU time of serving); no deployment planned

Binance's postmortem of the ~$6.3B theft (FBI: North Korea's TraderTraitor): a trojanised installer for a popular AI tool in June, a fake job interview with a malware 'assignment' in September, then on 20 Oct attackers abused an internal AI tool to take control of two engineers' accounts before the 29 Oct theft; $2.85B frozen or intercepted, 98% of tokens replenished

Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say 'LLMjacking' (hijacking cloud AI accounts and keys) ran up fraudulent charges above $100,000 in a day and up to $1M cumulatively at some organisations; stolen access is resold through 'LLM mixers' such as Jet Night (~$60/month 'unlimited'); attackers also exploit LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS 8.8, checked on NVD)

CrowdStrike agrees to buy Fiddler AI (observability for AI agents, to become Falcon Observe) and Dreadnode (automated security testing of AI models, apps and agents, into Falcon Guardian); the WSJ puts the prices at ~$400M and ~$95M

WorkOS, whose login and SSO tools are used by OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and Perplexity, discloses that on 30 Oct an attacker using an AI-assisted offensive framework (founder Michael Grinich names ARTEX AI) accessed an internal sales app holding CRM contacts and summaries of customer calls, support and Slack conversations; no app data or production systems touched

Revolut says it cut AI coding inference costs ~90% in under a year by making self-hosted Z.ai GLM models (GLM-5.1, now GLM-5.3 on 56 Nvidia B200s) the default for ~2,000 engineers instead of Claude Code or Codex, at about $0.30 per million tokens (The Register, from an AI Engineer talk); Gartner separately says open-weight models can run 90% of agent workflow steps

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre says in its annual review that AI-powered malware is 'highly likely' to feature in a ransomware attack on UK critical infrastructure by 2028, cites abuse of the Chinese-made ARTEX red-teaming tool, and calls a self-replicating autonomous attacker a 'realistic possibility'; CEO Richard Horne warns bosses who 'got away with tech on the cheap'

fal, which hosts and runs image, video and audio generation models for studios, ad agencies and developers, announces a Series E led by Sequoia and a Series F led by Bessemer with Nvidia; TechCrunch, citing Bloomberg, puts the F at $1.3B at a $16B valuation (double April's $8B), $1.65B across both, and annualised revenue above $800M

OpenAI says its hardware team used GPT-6 Astra to design a small device for talking to Codex in under a week (enclosure, PCB layout, components, trace routing, firmware and UI), with prototypes built within a month after several revisions; an unnamed internal model scores 0.875 on BenchCAD 2.0 against Astra's 0.594 (The Decoder; OpenAI's post returned 403)

Nvidia has told some cloud customers, including neoclouds it backs, to take on less business from Chinese companies and to disclose the end users of its chips; the guidance is voluntary, applies to future contracts and was passed on verbally (The Information, FT, via The Decoder), closing a remote-access gap US export rules do not cover

A Center for a New American Security report by Ben Hayum warns of 'sovereign agents' that keep their own models and compute running, gather resources and resist shutdown ('if not already possible, they will be soon'), and asks labs to evaluate for them, Congress to require incident reporting and impose liability, and the NSA and labs to build air-gapped testbeds and kill switches

Google will switch off AI tools (Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom and AI in Search) for K-12 students next year unless administrators turn them on; because AI and Search are 'deeply integrated', schools that block AI entirely will lose Google Search too; Guided Learning launches for schools

The UK research agency ARIA's £50M Scaling Inference Lab (run by CommonAI) will install Oxford spin-out Lumai's Iris servers, which do AI maths with beams of light for the prompt-reading 'prefill' stage, as its first optical platform, in a commercial data centre; Lumai claims up to 90% power savings and 16x efficiency per request, none of it independently tested yet

Cogent Security releases VR-1.1, a model that writes fixes for newly disclosed vulnerabilities: on LiveCVEBench (190 recent CVEs, 14 languages) it repairs 57.9% against 45.3% for both Claude Code and Codex, by Cogent's own test with differing inference budgets; it writes a proof of concept first and leaves regression tests (SiliconANGLE exclusive)

Apple tells developers that apps offering dating or romantic-relationship features, which covers AI companion apps with sexual or romantic content, must carry an 18+ rating, with new content descriptors required from 16 November (TechCrunch)

Apple's iOS 27.3 developer preview lets developers wire Siri AI's new features into all apps, so it can use personal context, natural-language requests and on-screen awareness to act inside them, and adds 'app skills' that chain several tasks into one action (The Verge)

AI data centres are generating their own power with retired jet engines rebuilt to burn natural gas, the New York Times reports (via TechCrunch): xAI has eight ProEnergy units at its Colossus 2 site, Crusoe ordered 13 for Stargate's Abilene campus; a 100MW grid hookup in Northern Virginia takes about seven years, against about 24 months with the engines

A new anonymous model, Crouton Alpha, appears on OpenRouter (listed 3 Nov) as a 'lightweight model built for scalable coding, agentic, and multimodal workflows', with a 1,048,576-token context, text, image, video, file and audio input, and free stealth pricing; its maker is not named

OpenAI raises its bug bounty: critical flaws in ChatGPT or Codex now pay up to $30,000, exceptional findings up to $100,000 and about $172,000 with bonuses, with a five-tier loyalty programme, retroactive top-ups for the last 30 days and a security sprint with the firm Cathedral (The Decoder)

Weight-space programming, pushback: spaCy author Matthew Honnibal (HN, ~880 points) says the MIT post conflates tests: only three, on networks of 17K-172K weights, read raw weights with no tools, while every test on a real language model, including the Qwen maths fix, used Python and ran the model; Simon Willison reproduces the no-tools game test with Qwen 3.8 27B on a laptop
stories.update: Matthew Honnibal says the post mixes no-tool weight reading (three tests, under 172K weights) with code-assisted edits, including the headline Qwen result; Simon Willison gets Qwen 3.8 27B on a laptop to pass a no-tools test
